meta.title: What Were We to Do?
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses rhetorical questions that make the reader feel the problem.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 107w at FK 6.1, part_2 105w at FK 7.0, part_3 102w at FK 4.4. The load is rhetorical questions and the school's money problem.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery (1901), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Washington, Booker T. Up from Slavery. 1901. Project Gutenberg eBook #2376, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2376, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: The authoring pass split long sentences, dropped rare words, moved one sentence to keep the parts balanced, and removed a dialect aside; no facts added.
source.survey: A school for freed people has more students than rooms and no money to buy a campus.
source.drafted_by: LessonBot harness (DeepSeek 1017), adapted from the human source; source review completed

session.difficulty_basis: rhetorical questions that make the reader feel the problem

authoring_exceptions: part_3 measures FK 4.4, just below the 4-5 window; the passage's short rhetorical questions carry the load, and splitting further would lose them.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: All these ideas and needs came at us at once, with a weight that seemed almost too much to bear. What were we to do? We had only the little old shack and the abandoned church that the good people of the town had kindly lent us for our teaching. The number of pupils was rising every day. The more we saw of them, and the more we went around the countryside, the more we saw that our work only partly did what the people really needed. These were the people we wanted to lift up by the pupils we should teach and send out to lead.
passage.part_2: The more we talked with the pupils, who came to us from many parts of the state, the more we found that many of them mostly wanted school so they would not have to work with their hands any longer. About three months after the school opened, when we were most anxious about our work, an old abandoned plantation came up for sale. It was about a mile from the town of Tuskegee. The mansion house—or “big house,” as it was called—had been burned. The owners had lived there during slavery. The old shack and the abandoned church were all the school had.
passage.part_3: We looked the place over carefully. It seemed just what we needed to make our work effective and permanent. But how were we to get it? The price was only five hundred dollars. But we had no money. We were strangers in town and had no credit. The owner agreed to let us occupy the place if we paid two hundred and fifty dollars down. The other two hundred and fifty dollars had to be paid within a year. Although five hundred dollars was cheap for the land, it was a large sum when one did not have any part of it.

items.prompt: In the opening, what two buildings did the school have for teaching? Name both places the passage gives.

tutor_only.confirm: The little old shack and the empty church lent by the town.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The third sentence of part_1 states that they had 'only the little old shack and the empty church that the good people of the town had kindly lent us for our teaching.'
tutor_only.tell: The passage names two places used for teaching. The sentence about the school lists both buildings.
help: Reread the third sentence of the opening.
That sentence lists the two places the school used for teaching.
tutor_only.core_idea: The school had only a small old shack and a borrowed empty church to teach in.
accept_ideas: the little old shack and the empty church
an old shack and a church the town lent them
the shack and the borrowed church
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They name the burned mansion house or the abandoned plantation.
if_they_say.ask: Which words in the opening did you use? Look again at the first lines.

items.prompt: The school had only a shack and an empty church. The number of pupils rose every day. How do these two facts connect to show the school's problem?

tutor_only.confirm: The two facts show the school had too little room for a growing number of pupils.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'We had only the little old shack and the empty church...' and the sentence 'The number of pupils was rising every day' carry the answer.
tutor_only.tell: The shack and church gave the school little room. Pupils kept arriving, so the space problem grew.
help: The school had only a shack and an empty church.
The number of pupils was rising every day.
tutor_only.core_idea: The school's small space could not fit the growing number of pupils.
accept_ideas: The school did not have enough room for the growing number of pupils.
The small shack and church became a problem as more pupils came.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the two facts show the pupils were poor.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence tells about the school's space?

items.prompt: The pupils wanted school so they would not have to work with their hands. What does that tell you about what they thought school was for?

tutor_only.confirm: They saw school as a way out of field work, not as learning for its own sake.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says many pupils wanted school so they would not have to work with their hands, which shows they saw it as an escape from field work.
tutor_only.tell: The passage says many pupils wanted school so they would not have to work with their hands. That shows they saw school as a way out of field work.
help: The plantation came up for sale near Tuskegee. Think about what that could offer the school.
The sale happened when the school was anxious. Say what that might mean.
tutor_only.core_idea: They saw school as an escape from field work, not as learning for its own sake.
accept_ideas: They wanted a way out of field work.
They saw school as an escape from farm work.
They did not want to work with their hands.
They thought school would lead to easier work.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the pupils wanted to learn for its own sake.
if_they_say.ask: What does the passage say the pupils wanted school for?

items.prompt: The writer asks, 'What were we to do?' instead of saying what they did. What does the question do that a statement would not?

tutor_only.confirm: It leaves the problem unanswered, instead of saying what they did.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Right after the needs crowd in, the writer asks 'What were we to do?' and does not say what they did, so the problem stays open.
tutor_only.tell: The writer asks what they could do and does not answer, so the problem stays open.
help: Find the question 'What were we to do?'
Notice that the next sentences do not answer it.
tutor_only.core_idea: The question leaves their problem unanswered, where a statement would have said what they did.
accept_ideas: it shows they did not know what to do
it shows they had no answer yet
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the question asks for a factual answer or a list of steps.
if_they_say.ask: Does the writer answer the question, or leave it open?

partial.when: the student says the question shows the leaders were worried or uncertain, without saying that nothing is answered
partial.ask: What does asking do here that telling would not?

items.prompt: The opening piles up needs. What does the last part narrow the problem to?

tutor_only.confirm: One property and one money problem.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part_1 carries the broad need: the pupils were rising and the work only partly met what people needed. Part_3 carries the shift to a concrete plan and obstacle: the abandoned plantation seemed what they needed, but the price was five hundred dollars, they had no money, and the owner required two hundred and fifty dollars down and the rest within a year.
tutor_only.tell: The opening lists many needs. The last part narrows them to one property and the money to buy it.
help: The need in the opening is broad and urgent.
The last part names a place, a price, and a payment problem.
tutor_only.core_idea: The last part narrows the broad needs to one property and one money problem.
accept_ideas: One piece of land and the money problem.
A single property and how to pay for it.
The plantation and the five hundred dollars.
not_required: Every detail about the pupils or the Alabama story
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the last part lists many needs again.
if_they_say.ask: What one property and what money problem does the last part name?
